edge.title: The price printed on the strip
edge.setup: At the chemist, or buying anything packaged, you pay the MRP without a thought. It is printed, official-looking and the same on every shelf, so it feels like the price. For a long-term medicine bought every month, the gap between that number and what the shop paid can be large.
edge.tell: MRP is the most a seller may charge, not what the product cost and not a price you have to pay.
move: Ask for the cheapest option with the same salt and strength, and compare the per-tablet price, not the brand.
For a medicine you buy monthly, price it at two or three chemists and a Jan Aushadhi Kendra before settling on one.
Take the bill every time, and treat a discount off MRP as normal to ask for, not a favour.
edge.why: The seller knows what the product cost; you see only a printed ceiling. When one side can see the cost and the other cannot, the ceiling quietly becomes the going price. Comparing on salt and strength puts back the information the label hides.
edge.variants: Same shape: 'MRP' on water and snacks at airports and venues, accessories sold at the full tag, 'sale' tags that cut from an inflated MRP.
edge.anchor: The Supreme Court questioned the overpricing of medicines and the massive gap between MRP and cost to retailers (Hindustan Times).

lens.name: Asymmetric information
lens.one_line: When one side knows much more than the other, the market degrades toward the worse goods.
lens.detail: If buyers can't tell good used cars from bad, they offer an average price. Owners of genuinely good cars refuse to sell at that price and leave the market, so the average quality drops, so the price drops further. Quality collapses — not from dishonesty, but from unverifiability. Every real fix is a verification mechanism: warranties, certification, inspection, reputation.
elsewhere: Freelance marketplaces race to the bottom without reviews.
Insurance pools get sicker when only the sick buy in.
A degree works partly as a costly signal of something an employer can't directly see.
lens.test: What can the other side see that I can't — and what would make it visible?
lens.today: The Supreme Court asked why the MRP on medicines sits so far above what retailers pay (Hindustan Times). The chemist sees the cost and you see only the printed ceiling, so that ceiling becomes the price. Asking for the same salt at a lower price is how you make the hidden number visible.

moved.what: Karnataka's final voter list after SIR is out: the electorate stands at 4.54 crore, nearly 1 crore fewer, with 65.45 lakh marked permanently shifted (The Times of India).
moved.so_what: Search your name in the final roll tonight. If you moved flats recently, you may be among those marked shifted, and finding out now beats finding out on polling day.

moved.what: Safety clearance for the Bannerghatta Road metro line was reported as likely today, and the Supreme Court has allowed BMRCL to go ahead with the Blue Line (Deccan Herald).
moved.so_what: A clearance is not an opening date. Keep your current commute until BMRCL announces a start, then try the line off-peak first.

moved.what: After an 18-month delay, Hennur–Bagalur road work has a December deadline and concretising works a two-month deadline; an elevated corridor or flyovers are also being considered (The Indian Express, Deccan Herald).
moved.so_what: Plan on the disruption lasting through December and treat the date as the earliest, not the likely finish. If your route uses it, test an alternative this week.

carry_over.prompt: Someone you barely know asks you to carry a sealed packet on your trip as a small favour: what is the problem with saying yes?
carry_over.answer: You are being asked to answer for contents you cannot verify, for a person who will not be there if it goes wrong.
